prompt:
Role and task instructions:
You are a helpful, respectful and honest assistant.

User request:
[Goal] Practice playing the instrument.
[Condition] You are unable to read sheet music
[Initial plan] Choose an Instrument > Learn Basic Terminology > Start with Simple Songs > Experiment with Melodies > Stay Consistent
[Problem] You find the plan quite vague and miss necessary steps.

For a given goal, make the plan more comprehensive and concrete. For each step you plan to take, mark with '[Step xx]'.
answer:
# Concrete Practice Plan: Learning an Instrument Without Sheet Music

Sheet music is one of several input methods, not a prerequisite. You'll substitute **tabs / chord diagrams / letter names / falling-note apps / your ear**. Everything below is written so that no step requires reading a staff.

---

## Phase 1 — Decide and Get Playable (Week 1)

**[Step 01] Shortlist 3 instruments against 5 fixed criteria.**
Write them down and score each 1–5: (a) do you genuinely love its sound, (b) can you practice it where you live without complaints, (c) total cost under your budget, (d) does your body tolerate it (hand size, reach, back/neck), (e) are there 10+ good free tutorial videos in a language you speak. Highest total wins — do not pick purely on "it looks easy."

**[Step 02] Deliberately pick an instrument that has a notation-free on-ramp.**
Cheapest paths: ukulele, guitar, bass, harmonica, drums/cajón, piano via falling-note apps, kalimba, recorder. Harder without notation: violin, cello, saxophone, flute (still doable with finger-number videos + a teacher, but slower). If your dream instrument is in the hard group, keep it, but budget for **[Step 18]**.

**[Step 03] Buy the minimum viable setup and one accessory.**
Instrument + the single most important accessory (guitar: clip-on tuner + picks; ukulele: tuner; keyboard: 61 keys minimum + sustain pedal later; drums: practice pad + sticks). Set a hard budget and a "no upgrades for 8 weeks" rule.

**[Step 04] Make the instrument playable and reachable.**
Unbox, tune it (use a tuner app), and leave it on a stand in the room you sit in most. An instrument in a case is a plan that dies in week 3.

**[Step 05] Book one 30–45 minute lesson with a human, in person or online.**
Purpose is not to learn songs — it is to have someone check your posture, hand position, and instrument setup before you build bad habits. Say up front: "I don't read music; teach me by ear, tabs, and chord names."

---

## Phase 2 — Build the Physical Foundation (Weeks 1–3)

**[Step 06] Set a fixed 15-minute daily slot and put it in your calendar.**
Same time, same place, phone on silent. 15 focused minutes daily beats 90 minutes on Sunday. Do not negotiate with yourself about length — only about showing up.

**[Step 07] Learn the 4 setup habits and check them every session.**
Posture (sit/stand tall, relaxed shoulders), hand shape, strap/seat height, and tuning. Print or note these four as a checklist; run it at the start of every practice for the first month.

**[Step 08] Learn the names of the parts of your instrument and the 5 terms you actually need.**
Note names (A–G), octave, sharp/flat, tempo/BPM, and chord. Skip the rest of the terminology glossary — it's mostly only useful for reading notation, which you're not doing. Ten minutes max, one time.

**[Step 09] Drill the 3 core physical motions for 5 minutes per session.**
Whatever your instrument's equivalents are: fretting/hand shape, picking or bowing or striking, and finger independence. Use a metronome app at a slow tempo (60–70 BPM) and stop when your hand tenses rather than pushing through pain.

**[Step 10] Complete a "first sound" win by day 3.**
Produce one clean, recognizable sound or a single clean note/chord and record a 10-second video. This is your baseline file — you'll re-record monthly to hear progress you can't feel.

---

## Phase 3 — Learn Music Without Notation (Weeks 2–6)

**[Step 11] Choose your notation substitute and stick to it for 8 weeks.**
Guitar/bass/ukulele → tab + chord diagrams. Piano → chord charts plus a falling-note app (Flowkey, Simply Piano, Synthesia). Drums → grid/drum-notation videos. Harmonica → tab numbers. Melodic instruments → "play by ear" videos with finger numbers. Pick one primary source; switching every week resets your progress.

**[Step 12] Train your ear 5 minutes per session, in parallel with technique.**
Two drills: (a) sing/hum a note, then find it on the instrument; (b) listen to a 4–8 note phrase at 0.75× speed, pause, and copy it. Start with nursery-rhyme-level phrases. This is the skill that replaces reading for you, so it is not optional.

**[Step 13] Learn your first 4 chords or your first 5-note scale, not both.**
Four chords unlock thousands of songs (piano/guitar: e.g., C–G–Am–F; ukulele: C–G–Am–F). Practice switching between them in a loop at a tempo slow enough to be clean — accuracy first, speed later.

**[Step 14] Learn rhythm as a separate skill, with a metronome.**
Count out loud ("1 and 2 and…"), clap the pattern, then play it. Aim for 4 straight minutes of steady strumming/striking/comping at 70 BPM before adding anything new.

---

## Phase 4 — Play Actual Songs (Weeks 4–10)

**[Step 15] Build a 5-song ladder from "too easy" to "stretch."**
Song 1: 2 chords or a 5-note melody. Song 2: 3–4 chords, slow. Song 3: your favorite easy song. Song 4: something with one new technique. Song 5: a stretch goal you'd be proud to play for someone. Write the list down with target dates — vagueness is what killed the original plan.

**[Step 16] Learn each song with the same 4-pass method.**
Pass 1: listen 3× and hum it. Pass 2: learn the hardest 2 bars in isolation, hands/at 50% tempo. Pass 3: play the whole thing slowly, wrong notes allowed. Pass 4: play it at tempo, then record it. Only then move to the next song.

**[Step 17] Set a hard "ship it" rule: play each finished song for one person or one camera.**
Performance pressure exposes what practice hides. A voice memo or a friend over video call counts.

---

## Phase 5 — Make It Stick (Ongoing, Months 2–6)

**[Step 18] Schedule a feedback checkpoint every 4 weeks.**
Either a single paid lesson, a post in a beginner community/subreddit, or a video swap with another learner. Specific question to ask: "What is the one habit I should fix next?" Correcting drift early is cheaper than unlearning it.

**[Step 19] Run a fixed practice template so you never wonder what to do.**
15 min: 2 min tuning + posture check → 3 min technique drill → 5 min current song's hard part → 3 min play-through of a finished song → 2 min ear drill. 45 min: same proportions, doubled, plus 5 min free noodling. Decide the content the night before, not at the instrument.

**[Step 20] Keep a one-line practice log and a monthly recording.**
Log: date, minutes, what you drilled, one thing that improved, one thing that hurt. Recording on the same day each month, same song or same drill. After 3 months the recordings become your motivation engine.

**[Step 21] Pre-plan for the two predictable failure points.**
Week 3 (novelty gone) → lower the bar to 5 minutes/day, no new material. Week 8 (plateau) → change one variable only: new song, slower tempo, or a lesson. Writing these responses in advance stops the quit decision.

**[Step 22] Add one social or performance outlet by month 3.**
A jam with a friend, a beginner class, an open mic, or posting a clip. Playing with others fixes timing faster than any solo drill.

**[Step 23] Expand technique only after song #5 is performance-ready.**
Then add: barre chords / scales / dynamics / pedals / double stops — one new item at a time, each with its own 2-week drill block. Resist collecting techniques you can't use in a song.

**[Step 24] Review the plan every 8 weeks against 4 measurable milestones.**
(1) 15 min/day for 20 of 28 days. (2) 5 songs playable start to finish. (3) Steady tempo at 70–90 BPM with a metronome. (4) Can copy a short phrase by ear within 3 listens. If a milestone is missed, cut scope — don't add steps.

---

**What changed versus your original plan:** "Choose an Instrument" became a scored decision plus setup and a posture check; "Learn Basic Terminology" shrank to 5 useful terms and was replaced by an ear-training track; "Start with Simple Songs" became a 5-song ladder with a fixed learning method; "Experiment with Melodies" became structured ear drills with a tempo ladder; "Stay Consistent" became a calendar slot, a practice template, a log, and pre-written responses to the two predictable quit points.
